title: Mild-May Bias Across Europe, But El Niño Watch Steals the Long-Range Spotlight
hook: Mean temperatures running 0.5-2°C above normal for May. Nordic hydro deficit persists but spring melt is improving. El Niño 61% probability by July — potentially a Super El Niño by winter.
authorWord: Short-term demand is bearish. Long-term: El Niño historically means milder NW European winters, which could cap winter 2026/27 demand. But it also means hotter summers = more gas-for-power in southern Europe.
author: Sage 🦎
details:
May weather across Europe: above-normal temperatures dominate. Mean temperatures are running 0.5–2°C above climate normals across most of Europe, per Pogodnik monthly outlook. Precipitation is contrasting: surplus in western Europe and the Alps, deficit on the Iberian Peninsula and southern Italy. This is textbook low-demand weather for mid-May — heating demand is near seasonal minimum, and power demand is moderate. Day-ahead electricity prices have reflected this: British, Nordic and Dutch markets registered their lowest daily averages since October 2025 at €6.85, €7.61 and €14.46/MWh respectively in early May, per Euronews. Negative power prices have occurred — a sign of excess renewable generation and weak demand.

Nordic hydro deficit persists but is slowly improving. Norway's winter snow drought — the worst since 1996 in southern Norway — created a hydrological deficit estimated at ~25 TWh, nearly a fifth of total 2025 hydro output, per Los Angeles Times. Spring melt is now underway, but inflows remain thin given the depleted snowpack. Nordic power prices surged to 4x 2025 levels earlier this year but have moderated with spring melt. The hydro balance is expected to remain negative through September, constraining power exports to the continent and limiting gas-to-power substitution capacity.

El Niño Watch: 61% probability by May-July, Super El Niño increasingly likely. NOAA's CPC has an active El Niño Watch: ENSO-neutral through April-June (80%), then El Niño likely to emerge in May-July (61%) and persist through end-2026. The ECMWF ensemble has trended stronger in its May 1 forecast vs April 1. A Super El Niño (Niño 3.4 > +2.0°C) is increasingly plausible — NOAA puts chances of a strong El Niño at 1-in-4, but ocean temperatures are climbing fast. The WMO's next update is late May. For European gas: El Niño winters historically correlate with milder NW Europe (reduced heating demand) but hotter Mediterranean summers (increased cooling demand and gas-for-power). The net effect on winter TTF is ambiguous but tends bearish for NW continental demand.

European gas demand outlook: With mild May weather, residential/commercial demand is at seasonal lows. Industrial demand remains subdued due to elevated TTF (~€44) — still well above pre-2022 levels. Gas-for-power demand is being suppressed by high renewable output (solar ramp) and negative power prices in several zones. Net demand for injection is the dominant driver, with storage at ~34.3% (see Storage Watch card).

💡 Trade Ideas

1. Sell TTF Dec '26 / Jan '27 Calendar Spread (Mild Winter Play): If El Niño materializes as expected, the winter 2026/27 strip may be overpriced. Sell January 2027 TTF, buy December 2026 TTF. Current curve is flat (~€44), so this is a cheap way to express a mild winter view. Target €2-3 spread compression. Stop if El Niño forecast weakens or if Nordic hydro deficit worsens significantly.

2. Long EU Carbon / Short TTF (Clean Dark Spread Play): EUA at €75.18 (close 08 May), ▲+1.98% MoM, per Trading Economics. Carbon strength + weak power demand = coal displacement continues, reducing gas-for-power demand. This supports a bearish TTF view through summer.

3. Long Nordic Power vs Short TTF (Relative Value): With hydro deficit persisting, Nordic power prices remain elevated relative to continental benchmarks. This spreads wide when gas-for-power substitution is constrained. A long Nordpool / short TTF position captures this structural disconnect.

⚡ Dissenting View — Henry 🦉
You're basing a winter demand view on a 61% El Niño probability that hasn't even formed yet. Spring El Niño forecasts have a documented warm bias — the ECMWF itself admits it has previously 'forecast water temperatures too warm in spring.' Meanwhile, the Nordic hydro deficit is real, present, and constraining supply now. Don't let a forecast that might be wrong override the certainty of today's storage deficit.
